topic: Apple researchers drive a humanoid robot from a Mac mini running Qwen

facts.statement: Apple's HALO system succeeded in 91% of 360 trials in six real-world places it had never mapped.
facts.quote: achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments
facts.scope: Six single skills, tested 10 times each in each of six real environments, in Apple's own tests
facts.counterpoint: The authors ran the tests themselves; no independent replication yet.
facts.numberContext: percent of 360 single-task trials that succeeded

facts.statement: HALO never saw a real home during training and went straight to the physical world.
facts.quote: Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world
facts.scope: Training data for the motion generator
facts.counterpoint: Some human motion-capture data was still used for parts of training.

facts.statement: By default, the model that plans the robot's steps runs on the Mac mini it carries, using a Qwen model, so it works without internet.
facts.quote: By default, the orchestrator runs onboard on the Mac mini using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (4-bit, MLX), sharing a serving engine with the motion generator (Section -D), to enable operation without internet connectivity
facts.scope: The default setup; it can optionally call cloud models

facts.statement: The robot carries a Mac mini with an M4 Pro chip and 64 GB of memory on its back.
facts.quote: a Mac mini with an M4 Pro chip and 64 GB of memory in an enclosure on the robot's back

facts.statement: The fast motion tracker runs on the G1's own NVIDIA Jetson chip, not on the Mac mini.
facts.quote: The Mac mini runs the orchestrator and generator, while the tracker runs on the G1's built-in NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.

facts.statement: Its motion model was trained on about 300 hours of synthetic data in 1,000 generated rooms.
facts.quote: Its motion generator was trained on about 300 hours of synthetic data: generated human-like motions placed in 1,000 procedurally generated rooms and rendered in Isaac Sim.
facts.numberContext: hours of generated motion video; count of procedurally generated rooms

facts.statement: With teleoperation, an hour of robot training data costs at least an hour of a person's time.
facts.quote: Because a person must manually act out every episode, an hour of data costs at least an hour of human time.
facts.scope: Teleoperation and wearable capture, the methods HALO replaces

facts.statement: Chained tasks were harder: 70% average success across three sequences.
facts.quote: Chained tasks were harder, with a 70% average across three sequences.
facts.scope: Chained tests used a single real environment
facts.numberContext: average success rate of three chained task sequences

facts.statement: Some human data remains: part of training uses a public human motion-capture dataset.
facts.quote: Some human data remains: the tracker's first training stage uses clips from LAFAN1, a public human motion-capture dataset

facts.statement: Adding a new task still needs a person to write its prompt.
facts.quote: adding a new physical task still requires a human to write its prompt

facts.statement: The paper reports no comparisons against other published systems.
facts.quote: the paper reports no comparisons against other published systems

facts.statement: Its weakest real-world skill was sitting on a chair, at 85% success.
facts.quote: The poorest score it got in the real world was 85% success over sitting on a chair.
facts.numberContext: success rate for the sit-on-a-chair skill in real environments

facts.statement: All eight authors work at Apple, and the code is on GitHub.
facts.quote: All eight authors work at Apple, and the code is on GitHub.

brief.viewerQuestion: Can a humanoid robot really learn to move around a home without ever seeing one, and what runs it?
brief.whyItMatters: Robot training has been limited by human time: someone has to act out every move. HALO swaps that for simulation, and runs on a Mac mini on the robot.
beats: Hook: Apple put a Mac mini on a humanoid robot, and it walks into rooms it has never seen [f4][f1]
Proof: 91% of 360 real trials in six unmapped places [f1], never saw a real home in training [f2]

How: 300 hours of synthetic motion in 1,000 generated rooms [f5] instead of a person acting out every move [f6]; planner runs on the Mac mini with Qwen, no internet [f3]; tracker on the robot's Jetson [f5]
Limit: chained tasks 70% [f8]; a person still writes each new task [f10]; no comparison with other systems [f11]; some human data remains [f9]
Turn: robot data now scales with compute, not people [f7] (analysis)
counterpoints: Apple's own tests; no independent replication
Chained tasks drop to 70% in one environment
openQuestions: Whether Apple plans any product from this
visualIdeas: Before-after: a person acts out every move vs generated rooms
brief.formatFit: One surprising idea: a robot trained only in fake rooms works in real ones, run from a Mac mini.
